hints: Look closely at statement 1 and picture a triglyceride: glycerol plus three fatty acid tails with no phosphate group. Does that give it two different regions like a membrane lipid?

Compare the two ways we break down a triglyceride: hydrolysis with water in digestion versus oxidation in respiration. Which one uses water and which one releases lots of energy and metabolic water from C-H bonds?
walkthrough:
**Test statement 1 - Is a triglyceride part hydrophobic, part hydrophilic?**

Think side by side with a phospholipid. A phospholipid has a hydrophilic phosphate head and hydrophobic tails, perfect for membranes.

A triglyceride has glycerol joined to three fatty acids and no charged head, so the whole molecule is non-polar and hydrophobic. Statement 1 is false.

**Test statement 2 - Why is it such a good energy store?**

The main function of triglyceride is as a concentrated energy reserve in adipose tissue and seeds.

Fatty acid tails are long hydrocarbon chains packed with $C-H$ bonds. Oxidation of these bonds in respiration releases a large amount of energy per gram, much more than carbohydrate. Statement 2 is true and really explains its function.

**Test statement 3 - Does hydrolysis release water?**

This is the classic trap. Hydrolysis means breaking ester bonds by *adding* water:
$$triglyceride + 3H_2O \rightarrow glycerol + 3 \text{ fatty acids}$$

Metabolic water is released later when those products are *oxidised* in aerobic respiration, not by hydrolysis. Statement 3 is false, so only 2 is correct.

options.A: Includes statement 1, but triglycerides are entirely hydrophobic with no hydrophilic region, unlike phospholipids.
options.B: Includes both 1 and 3, but 1 describes phospholipids and 3 confuses hydrolysis (which uses water) with oxidation (which releases water).
options.C: Includes statement 3, but hydrolysis consumes water. Metabolic water comes from oxidative respiration, not hydrolysis.
options.D: Correct, only statement 2 is true. The high proportion of C-H bonds gives a high energy yield on oxidation, ideal for energy storage.
